claims.text: Increasing annealing temperature changes the grain-boundary density of as-deposited HEA coatings.
Increasing annealing temperature changes the nanoscale phase distribution of as-deposited HEA coatings.
Annealing can optimize the balance between coating hardness and lubricious-phase formation.
The annealing-induced microstructural balance enhances wear resistance relative to the unannealed state.
The initial coatings are multiphase and nanostructured.
The initial coatings lack optimized grain-boundary structures.
Annealing temperature will be varied from the as-deposited condition through several intermediate steps up to a limit preceding coarsening.
HEA protective coatings can be produced by APS or laser cladding.
Secondary FCC or other nanoscale strengthening phases can modify local lubrication and hardening.
Annealing promotes atomic diffusion that causes phase transformations and grain-boundary engineering.
An optimum annealing-temperature window increases coating hardness.
Annealing-induced lubricious phases reduce friction during wear.
Insufficient annealing fails to produce the beneficial microstructural changes, whereas excessive annealing causes coarsening and degraded wear performance.
Coatings annealed at intermediate temperatures will have statistically significantly lower wear rates and friction coefficients than as-deposited coatings.
Improved wear performance will correspond to a refined microstructure with enhanced grain boundaries and nanoscale phases.
As-deposited HEA coatings typically have a less optimized microstructure than appropriately annealed coatings.
The proposed mechanism should apply to coatings made by APS and laser cladding within a moderate annealing range before excessive grain growth.
Wear results and the optimal annealing response may vary with alloy composition and processing history.
Wear rate and coefficient of friction are measurable indicators of coating wear performance.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear improvement or a correlation between the proposed microstructural mediators and wear performance would falsify the hypothesis.
